questionText: Listen to an advisor presenting information about studying abroad at a university info session.
audioScript:
Situation: A study abroad advisor gives an information session to second-year students considering a semester overseas.
Advisor: Good afternoon, everyone. I'm Dr Helen Carter, the study abroad coordinator here at Westfield University. Today I'll walk you through the key steps for applying to study abroad in your third year.
Advisor: We currently partner with forty universities across eighteen countries. The most popular destinations are Canada, Australia, and Germany, but I'd encourage you to look beyond the obvious choices.
Advisor: Applications open on the first of October and close on the fifteenth of December. You'll need to submit a personal statement of five hundred words, two academic references, and your most recent transcript.
Student: Excuse me, is there a minimum grade requirement?
Advisor: Yes, you must hold at least a sixty per cent average in your current modules. Some partner universities ask for sixty-five, so check the specific requirements.
Advisor: There are two types of placement. The exchange programme means you pay no tuition fees to the host university, only your usual fees here. The study abroad programme means you pay tuition to the host institution directly.
Advisor: Funding is available through the Global Mobility Bursary, worth up to fifteen hundred pounds, awarded on a competitive basis. The deadline for bursary applications is the end of February.
Advisor: Finally, you must attend a pre-departure workshop in May, which covers visas, health insurance, and cultural adjustment. If you have questions afterwards, email me at the study abroad office.

questionText: Listen to a facilities manager giving a tour of the university sports centre.
audioScript:
Situation: A sports facilities manager shows new members around the university sports centre during an induction tour.
Manager: Hi folks, I'm Greg, the facilities manager here at the Oakfield Sports Centre. Welcome aboard. Let me show you what we offer.
Manager: On this ground floor we have the main sports hall, which is marked out for badminton, basketball, and indoor cricket. It can be split into four courts at once.
Manager: Through those doors is the twenty-five-metre swimming pool. Lane swimming runs from six in the morning until eight, and again from noon to two.
Student: Is the pool open every day?
Manager: Every day except Sunday, when we only run family sessions from ten until four.
Manager: Upstairs you'll find the fitness suite with forty stations, including treadmills, rowing machines, and free weights. You must complete a free induction before using it, which takes about forty-five minutes.
Manager: We also offer fitness classes: spin, yoga, and circuits. Each class lasts an hour and costs three pounds for members.
Manager: Membership for students is one hundred and twenty pounds per year, or you can pay as you go at four pounds per visit. Membership includes the pool, the sports hall, and the fitness suite.
Manager: Lockers are available in the changing rooms. Bring your own padlock, or hire one from reception for a two-pound deposit.
Manager: Any questions? Drop by the reception any time between seven and ten, seven days a week.

questionText: Listen to a transport officer explaining public transport options to new students.
audioScript:
Situation: A city transport officer briefs new university students on using public transport around the city.
Officer: Morning everyone. I'm Sandra, a transport officer with CityBus. I'm here to help you get around affordably as students. Let's cover the essentials.
Officer: The city has three main bus routes serving the university. The number seven runs every ten minutes and goes straight to the city centre. The number twelve runs every fifteen minutes and reaches the shopping district. The number twenty-three runs every twenty minutes and connects to the train station.
Student: How much does a single ticket cost?
Officer: A standard single is one pound eighty for adults, but with a student SmartCard it drops to one pound twenty.
Officer: I'd recommend the term pass. It costs ninety pounds and covers unlimited travel on all CityBus routes for thirteen weeks. Compared with pay-as-you-go, most students save about thirty pounds a term.
Officer: The SmartCard itself is free, but you need a passport photo and your student ID to register at the travel centre on Market Street. Registration takes about ten minutes.
Officer: Buses run from five in the morning until midnight, Monday to Saturday. On Sundays, services start at eight and finish at ten in the evening.
Officer: There's also a night bus, the N7, running every thirty minutes from midnight to four, mainly for safety. It follows the same route as the number seven but costs two pounds fifty regardless of your card.
Officer: Lost SmartCards can be replaced for a five-pound fee at the travel centre, and your remaining balance transfers automatically.

questionText: Listen to a librarian explaining how to sign up for library skills workshops.
audioScript:
Situation: A librarian explains the schedule and booking process for a series of library skills workshops to first-year students.
Librarian: Hello, and welcome to Greenfield Library. I'm Marcus, and I run the library skills workshop programme. Let me tell you how to get the most from these sessions.
Librarian: We offer five workshops this term, each focused on a different skill. The first is Introduction to Referencing, running in week two. The second is Avoiding Plagiarism, in week three. Then Database Searching in week four, Critical Reading in week five, and finally Literature Reviews in week six.
Student: Do we need to attend all five?
Librarian: They're optional, but I strongly recommend at least the first three. They build on one another, so the order matters.
Librarian: Each workshop lasts ninety minutes and takes place in Seminar Room B on the second floor. The maximum group size is twenty, so places are limited.
Student: How do we sign up?
Librarian: Bookings open online one week before each session. Go to the library website, log in with your student ID, and select the workshop. You'll get a confirmation email within twenty-four hours.
Librarian: If a session is full, you can join the waiting list. When a place opens up, you'll receive an automatic email and have forty-eight hours to confirm.
Librarian: There's no charge for any workshop. However, if you book and fail to attend without cancelling twenty-four hours in advance, a penalty flag is placed on your account, and you must wait one week before booking another session.
Librarian: Certificates of completion are issued if you attend at least four of the five workshops, which can be added to your CV.

questionText: Listen to a dining services manager presenting the campus meal plan options to students.
audioScript:
Situation: A dining services manager presents the campus dining plan options to new students at an orientation session.
Manager: Good afternoon. I'm Diane, manager of Campus Dining Services. I'll explain the meal plans available this year so you can choose what suits you best.
Manager: We offer three plans: the Basic, the Standard, and the Unlimited. Each works with your student card, which you top up or load a plan onto at the dining office.
Manager: The Basic Plan costs nine hundred pounds per semester and gives you ten meals per week plus one hundred pounds of flex dollars to spend at campus cafés.
Student: What's included in the Standard Plan?
Manager: The Standard Plan costs twelve hundred pounds per semester. It gives you fifteen meals per week plus two hundred and fifty flex dollars. This is our most popular option.
Manager: The Unlimited Plan costs fifteen hundred pounds per semester and offers all-you-can-eat access to the main dining hall during opening hours, plus one hundred flex dollars.
Manager: Unused meals don't roll over to the next week on the Basic and Standard plans. Flex dollars, however, carry over from the first semester to the second, but expire at the end of the academic year.
Manager: The main dining hall, located next to the science block, serves breakfast from seven to nine, lunch from eleven thirty to two, and dinner from five to seven thirty.
Manager: We accommodate dietary requirements. Vegetarian and vegan options are available at every meal. Halal and kosher meals require forty-eight hours' notice through the dining portal.
Manager: You can change your plan once per semester, free of charge, until the end of the second week of classes. After that, a twenty-pound administration fee applies.
Manager: Finally, guests can eat at the dining hall by paying eight pounds at the door, but they must be accompanied by a meal-plan holder.

questionText: Listen to a student union officer introducing the university's student clubs to freshers.
audioScript:
Situation: A student union officer introduces the range of student clubs and societies to first-year students at a fresher welcome event.
Officer: Hi everyone, I'm Olivia, vice president of the Student Union here at Kingsmere University. Welcome to clubs night. Let me give you a quick overview before you browse the stalls.
Officer: We have over a hundred and twenty clubs registered this year, split into five categories: academic, cultural, sporting, special interest, and volunteering. Each club sets its own membership fee, but the average is around fifteen pounds per year.
Student: Can we join more than one club?
Officer: Absolutely, you can join as many as you like. However, I'd suggest starting with two or three so you don't overcommit, especially in your first term.
Officer: To join, visit the club's stall tonight, fill in a short form, and pay the fee by card or cash. You'll get a membership sticker for your student card within five working days.
Officer: Most clubs hold their main meetings on Wednesday afternoons, since the university keeps that slot free for activities. A few, like the debating society and the film club, meet on Tuesday or Thursday evenings instead.
Officer: Every club must re-register with the Union each September. If a club fails to attract at least ten members by the end of October, its funding is reviewed and it may be dissolved.
Officer: Union funding is allocated based on membership numbers and activity level. The minimum grant is fifty pounds, and the maximum is five hundred pounds per year. Applications open in November.
Officer: A word on safety: all club trips off-campus require a risk assessment submitted to the Union two weeks in advance, signed by the club president. Insurance is provided through the Union's blanket policy, but personal equipment is not covered.
Officer: That's the basics. Stalls are open until eight, so take your time and ask questions. I'll be at the Union desk if you need me.

questionText: Listen to a sustainability officer leading a tour of the campus green initiatives.
audioScript:
Situation: A sustainability officer leads a small group of students on a tour of the campus environmental initiatives and facilities.
Officer: Welcome, everyone. I'm James, the campus sustainability officer here at Eastlake University. Today's tour covers our main green projects. We'll walk for about forty minutes, so wear comfortable shoes.
Officer: Our first stop is the solar array on the roof of the engineering block. Installed in twenty twenty-two, it generates about forty per cent of that building's electricity. We're planning to expand it to cover the library roof next summer.
Student: How much did the solar panels cost to install?
Officer: The initial installation cost two hundred thousand pounds, but we expect to recover that within eight years through energy savings.
Officer: Next, we have the rainwater harvesting system behind the sports hall. It collects water from the roof, stores it in a ten-thousand-litre tank, and supplies the irrigation system for the campus grounds. This reduces our mains water use by roughly twenty-five per cent.
Officer: We also run a comprehensive recycling scheme. There are four streams: paper, plastics, glass, and food waste. Food waste is sent to an anaerobic digester, which converts it into biogas used to heat the student residences.
Officer: The campus cycling scheme offers free bike loans for up to two weeks, with a refundable deposit of fifty pounds. After two weeks, rentals are two pounds per day. We currently have sixty bikes available across three docking stations.
Officer: Our latest project is the biodiversity garden, planted last spring near the lake. It features native wildflowers and a pollinator corridor, and is maintained by student volunteers. Volunteers commit to two hours per fortnight and can log it on their skills transcript.
Officer: Looking ahead, our target is to reach carbon neutrality by twenty thirty-five. The main challenge is heating: most buildings still rely on gas boilers, and switching to heat pumps requires significant investment.
Officer: If you want to get involved, sign up at the sustainability office or email green@eastlake.ac.uk. We meet on the first Thursday of each month.
